intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 (CMS11), associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency, is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RAPSN gene, which encodes rapsyn.

paragraphs.text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 is an autosomal recessive disorder of neuromuscular transmission. It results from a deficiency of acetylcholine receptor (AChR) at the motor endplate, caused by defects in rapsyn, a postsynaptic protein that concentrates and anchors AChR in the postsynaptic membrane (Ohno et al., 2002; Engel et al., 2015). Most patients present in the first year of life. Arthrogryposis and other congenital malformations occur in about one-third of patients, and intercurrent infections can trigger respiratory crises (Engel et al., 2015). Burke et al. (2003) distinguished an early-onset form from a late-onset form that begins in adolescence or adulthood.

checks.explanation: Recessive mutations causing a myasthenic syndrome (a neuromuscular transmission disorder).

paragraphs.text: Goldhammer et al. (1990) described 14 Jewish patients of Iraqi or Iranian origin, from 10 families, who had congenital myasthenia with facial malformations: an elongated face, mandibular prognathism with class III malocclusion, and a high-arched palate. Muscle weakness was mostly limited to ptosis, weakness of the facial and masticatory muscles, and fatigable speech. The course was mild and nonprogressive, and the patients responded to cholinesterase inhibitors. Antibodies to acetylcholine receptor were absent. Repetitive stimulation at 3 Hz produced a decremental response, but a single nerve stimulus did not evoke a repetitive compound muscle action potential. The authors suggested that the facial abnormalities might be secondary to the neuromuscular defect, or might be primary and unrelated.

paragraphs.text: Das et al. (2014) reported a 20-month-old boy with rapsyn deficiency. At birth he had a weak cry, hypotonia, joint contractures, and facial deformity. Respiratory difficulty associated with muscle fatigue kept him for a total of 71 days in the neonatal intensive care unit and 47 days in the pediatric intensive care unit. Imaging, a battery of metabolic tests, and electrodiagnostic studies were normal. Muscle biopsy showed myofiber atrophy in a pattern consistent with early denervation.

paragraphs.text: In a review, Engel et al. (2015) noted that most patients with rapsyn deficiency present in the first year of life and a few present later. Arthrogryposis at birth and other congenital malformations occur in nearly one-third of patients. Intercurrent infections or fever can trigger respiratory crises that lead to anoxic encephalopathy. The clinical features can suggest autoimmune myasthenia gravis, but ocular ductions are intact in most patients. Weakness occasionally has a limb-girdle and axial distribution.

paragraphs.text: Menold et al. (1998) studied 5 families of Iranian Jewish origin with 6 affected individuals, all diagnosed with a phenotypically distinct form of congenital myasthenic syndrome. Four of the families were consanguineous, and all came from the same geographic region. Linkage was excluded to the regions of chromosomes 2 and 17 that contain the AChR subunit genes, and to the region of chromosome 17p to which familial infantile myasthenia had been localized. The authors concluded that a defect in a different gene was responsible for the disorder in these patients.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2002) studied 4 patients with endplate AChR deficiency who had no mutations in the AChR subunit genes, and identified 3 recessive mutations in the RAPSN gene. One patient was compound heterozygous for leu14-to-pro (L14P), located in tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) 1, and asn88-to-lys (N88K), located in TPR3. Two patients were homozygous for N88K. The fourth patient carried N88K and a 5-bp insertion (553ins5) that causes a frameshift in TPR5. In each case, endplate studies showed decreased staining for rapsyn and AChR and impaired postsynaptic morphologic development. Expression studies in HEK cells showed that none of the mutations hindered rapsyn self-association, but all 3 diminished coclustering of AChR with rapsyn.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2003) identified 2 mutations in E-box elements of the RAPSN promoter region in 8 patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome. Patient 1 carried a -27C-G mutation that changes the E-box at -27 to -22 from CAGCTG to GAGCTG. The allele carrying -27C-G was not transcribed in the patient's muscle. Patients 2 through 8 were Oriental Jews of Iraqi or Iranian origin with facial malformations. They were homozygous for a -38A-G mutation that changes another E-box at -40 to -35 from CAACTG to CAGCTG without altering the CANNTG consensus sequence. Haplotype analysis indicated that -38A-G arose from a common founder. In electrophoretic mobility shift assays, -38A-G gained binding affinity and -27C-G lost binding affinity for different components of nuclear extracts from C2C12 myotubes. In luciferase reporter assays, both mutations attenuated reporter gene expression in C2C12 myotubes. The -27C-G mutation also attenuated expression in HEK cells transfected with MyoD or myogenin, and markedly reduced the enhancer activity of an E-box on an SV40 promoter. The authors predicted that the impaired transcriptional activity would reduce rapsyn expression and cause endplate AChR deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Gaudon et al. (2010) studied 3 patients with a characteristic phenotype of recessive congenital myasthenic syndrome and RAPSN mutations. In each, family analysis showed that the mutation on one allele had not been detected by direct sequencing. Allelic quantification of patient DNA identified 3 novel multiexon deletions of RAPSN. These rearrangements accounted for 15% of the authors' patients with RAPSN mutations, and the authors recommended gene dosage methods in addition to direct sequencing.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2003) identified a -27C-G mutation in the RAPSN promoter in a patient with congenital myasthenic syndrome. The mutation changes the E-box at -27 to -22 from CAGCTG to GAGCTG, and the allele carrying it was not transcribed in the patient's muscle. The mutation lost binding affinity for components of C2C12 myotube nuclear extracts. It attenuated reporter gene expression both in C2C12 myotubes and in HEK cells transfected with MyoD or myogenin, and markedly attenuated the enhancer activity of an E-box on an SV40 promoter.
